domain: International Law / Political Philosophy / Security Studies
topic_summary: Analysis of the contested interpretation of UN Charter provisions governing state sovereignty versus humanitarian intervention. The Charter's Article 2(7) non-intervention principle and Chapter VII enforcement powers create a structural tension between sovereignty-as-shield and human-rights-as-override, manifesting in divergent readings that produce incompatible constraints on legitimate use of force.

key_entities: UN Charter Article 2(7) (non-intervention in domestic jurisdiction)
UN Charter Chapter VII (Security Council enforcement powers)
key_tensions: State sovereignty as inviolable vs humanitarian obligations as override
Territorial integrity norm vs mass atrocity prevention imperative

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: UN Charter Article 2(7) non-intervention principle + Chapter VII enforcement powers create structural ambiguity about conditions legitimizing coercive intervention in sovereign states
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Security Council holds formal interpretive authority through Chapter VII resolutions; P5 veto concentrates authorization power; competing doctrinal schools (sovereignty-first vs R2P) claim authoritative interpretation

readings.authority_grounding: Westphalian state system; post-colonial sovereignty protection; UN Charter Article 2(7) plain text
readings.expected_structural_delta: High epsilon blocking intervention; beneficiaries are post-colonial/authoritarian states; victims are populations under domestic atrocity

readings.commitment: Sovereignty conditional on protecting populations; systematic atrocity triggers international responsibility to intervene
readings.authority_grounding: Universal human rights obligations; Genocide Convention; emerging customary international law
readings.expected_structural_delta: High epsilon legitimizing intervention; beneficiaries are persecuted populations; victims are targeted states and sovereignty norm itself

axiom_contradictions.basis: Sovereignty-first holds state consent as necessary condition for intervention legitimacy; R2P holds mass atrocity as sufficient condition overriding consent requirement. No single coherent framework can simultaneously require state consent and permit intervention over state objection in atrocity scenarios.
